fact_text: Service Long March Tyres is a joint venture between China's Long March and Pakistan's Service Industries and is Pakistan's first manufacturer of radial truck and bus tyres.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Commercial production began in March 2022 with an initial capacity of only about 7,400 tyres per year, which was expanded in stages to roughly 1.6 million tyres per year.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst frames the company as the flagship example of CPEC 2.0: instead of Chinese infrastructure investment, a Chinese export manufacturer relocates production to Pakistan and exports to the world.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The venture traces to 2017, when US anti-dumping duties on Chinese exports under Trump pushed Chinese manufacturers into a 'China plus one' strategy of building plants outside China.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Tyre exports scaled from roughly 135,000 units in FY23 to about 327,000 in FY24 and 434,000 in FY25, with around 300,000 shipped in the first half of FY26 alone.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Cars and bikes typically need new tyres roughly every two years, but trucks and buses replace tyres two or three times a year because of much higher running, making commercial tyres a high-frequency consumable.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan has roughly 500,000 trucks and buses, implying annual demand of about 4 to 5 million commercial tyres, historically met almost entirely by imported and smuggled tyres.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Radial truck tyres are the premium category: they last longer, carry more load and improve truck fuel efficiency, so transport fleets worldwide are gradually shifting from bias to radial tyres.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Natural rubber, synthetic rubber and carbon black are the main tyre inputs and are largely imported, and Pakistan applies almost zero import duty on natural and synthetic rubber.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Smuggled tyres avoid sales tax and duty but carry their own costs - extra freight via circuitous routes, border movement and payments at each stage - which is why a low-cost local plant can price against them.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst argues the company beats smuggled imports because a transporter gets all-steel radial technology plus a warranty and reliable supply at roughly the same price as mostly bias-type smuggled tyres.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Within about three years of starting up, the company captured roughly 43 percent of Pakistan's domestic truck-and-bus radial tyre market.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: By December 2025 about PKR 30 billion had been invested in the 1.6 million-tyre plant, worth roughly USD 150 million because part was spent when the rupee was near 160 per dollar.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst estimates roughly PKR 7,000 profit per tyre on about 1.5 million tyres, giving PKR 9-10 billion of annual profit and a dollarised return on invested capital of about 20 to 22 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The plant sits in the Nooriabad Special Economic Zone, where income tax exemptions are available until 2032, which materially lifts the company's after-tax returns.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst notes the replacement cost of a modern tyre plant of this scale is roughly USD 200-250 million while the IPO valued the company near USD 550 million, so investors paid about 2 to 2.5 times plant value.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's rule is that paying a premium over replacement cost is justified only when a business earns a very high return on invested capital, because future expansions then compound that return for the new owner.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Tyre manufacturing is energy intensive and electricity is a major cost line, so captive renewable generation is a direct margin lever for a tyre maker.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The company invested in renewable power including a 7.5 MW wind turbine, which the analyst expects to bring its electricity cost down to around 7 US cents per unit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On assumptions of 2 million tyres of capacity by end-2026 and a 55 percent local / 45 percent export mix, the analyst models 2027 revenue of PKR 85-87 billion, gross profit of PKR 21-22 billion and profit after tax of PKR 16-18 billion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Finance cost stays manageable for a capital-intensive manufacturer because the company uses concessional LTFF and export refinance facilities priced around 4.5 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The IPO raised roughly PKR 7.8 billion, earmarked for a passenger car radial tyre plant of about 3 million tyres a year costing around PKR 22.5 billion, with production expected by 2028.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Around 250,000 new cars are sold in Pakistan each year, implying about 1 million tyres of original-equipment demand, with a replacement market that is much larger again.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst sees currency as the biggest risk because rubber and carbon black are imported, but judges the hit smaller than for a purely domestic maker since a large share of output is exported and earns dollars.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Export markets act as a demand shock absorber: if local demand slows the company can lift export orders quickly, at somewhat lower margins, helped by its Chinese partner's global export network.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The government cut the super tax on local companies from 10 percent to 8 percent and has signalled further reductions plus eventual removal for exporters, which lowers the future tax burden on manufacturers.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Service Long March Tyres IPO: How Pakistan's Fastest IPO Could Hit $1 Billion' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan Aluminium Beverage Cans is the country's first and still only aluminium beverage can maker, supplying Pepsi and Coca-Cola as well as local brands such as Cola Next and Gourmet Cola.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Beverage companies are gradually shifting from glass and plastic bottles to aluminium cans, a global FMCG trend driven by environmental pressure to cut plastic waste, which structurally grows can demand.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Capacity rose from roughly 700 million cans a year in 2017 to about 1.2 billion cans a year after successive expansions.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A significant part of the company's volume is exported to Afghanistan, and it has sold more cans into Afghanistan than into Pakistan.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst frames the economics simply: roughly USD 100 million total invested in a 1.1-1.2 billion can plant, which at about PKR 5 profit per can and 85 percent utilisation produces around PKR 5 billion of annual profit.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Imported aluminium cans face roughly 36 percent of duties in Pakistan - 20 percent customs duty, 6 percent additional customs duty and 10 percent regulatory duty - plus anti-dumping duties of 20 to 26 percent on some origins.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because import duties let the company price locally above export prices, profit per can is materially higher at home, so investors should watch the local-versus-export sales mix rather than total volume alone.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The plant is in the Faisalabad special economic zone with income tax exemption to around 2027-2028; without it the analyst estimates profit per can would fall from about PKR 5 to roughly PKR 3.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Demand is highly seasonal: local volume is concentrated in Punjab and KPK and exports in Afghanistan, all cold-winter regions, so winter quarters are structurally weak and quarterly results must be read seasonally.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: After the Pakistan-Afghanistan border closed in October 2025, quarterly revenue fell from about PKR 7.4 billion in the September 2025 quarter to roughly PKR 3 billion in the December 2025 quarter.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The same border closure flipped profitability: about PKR 1.7 billion of profit before tax in the July-September 2025 quarter became a loss of roughly PKR 300 million in the following three months.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Revenue recovered to roughly PKR 3.7 billion in the first quarter of 2026 as the company looked for export markets outside Afghanistan.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst runs two scenarios: the Afghan border reopening and the business recovering, or the border staying shut while alternative markets such as Bangladesh or Central Asia are developed at lower profitability.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Afghan exports carried only moderately lower margins because Afghanistan has no can or plastic bottle plants of its own and the Faisalabad plant is the closest factory to Kabul, its main demand centre.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst sizes annual can demand at about 1.5 billion in Afghanistan versus only around 350 million in Pakistan, where single-serve plastic bottles dominate and cans hold just 10-12 percent of a 3 billion-plus unit market.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A can line only becomes cost-feasible at around 700-800 million cans of capacity, so with one incumbent already holding about a billion cans of capacity a second Pakistani plant is unlikely until local demand approaches a billion cans.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Faisalabad to Kabul is roughly 1,000 km direct, but routing through Iran stretches it to about 4,000 km, which diesel costs make uneconomic as a workaround for a closed Afghan border.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In 2025 the company announced an aluminium can plant inside Afghanistan, and it has continued the project despite the border disruption, which would cut transport cost and reduce border-closure risk.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The company's local pricing power depends on the roughly 36 percent import duty, so Pakistan's IMF-linked tariff rationalisation programme is a direct threat to profit per can if duties are cut materially.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Inside Pakistan's $300M Beverage Can Market – PABC Analysis' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan runs a single-buyer power model: listed generators contract with the government, cannot sell electricity to third parties, and the government dispatches them at will.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: IPPs recover debt service and their equity return through a fixed capacity payment, and pass fuel through at cost, so a plant generating cheap electricity does not necessarily earn more than an expensive one.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Most Pakistani power plants are financed roughly 75 percent debt and 25 percent equity, and the government guarantees a dollarised return of about 15 to 20 percent on the equity portion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's shortcut for any IPP is to multiply the equity invested by a capacity factor - about 25 percent for a 15 percent dollarised return and 30 percent for a Thar coal project - to get the real take-home income.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst applies his rule to Hubco's 330 MW Thar coal plant: roughly USD 125 million of equity in a plant on a 30 percent capacity factor implies around USD 37 million a year of distributable return on equity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Gross profit margin is meaningless for an IPP: because fuel is passed through at cost, higher dispatch inflates revenue and crushes the margin percentage while the gross profit amount barely moves, and an idle plant shows nearly 100 percent margin.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In an IPP's early years roughly half the capacity payment is debt repayment, so reported profit can look about double the sustainable level until the debt is amortised.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst evaluates every power company on two things only: its capacity to pay dividends, derived from plant cost and equity return, and the sponsor's willingness to pay, judged over at least five years of dividend history.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Under a 2021 agreement with the government, IPP capacity payments were converted into rupees and future payments put on a fixed basis.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Lalpir Power is a furnace-oil plant whose annual capacity payment is roughly PKR 9-10 per share, with the same sponsor group as Pakgen Power, and it has paid out about half of profits as dividends over five years.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Nishat Chunian Power and Nishat Power are near-identical 200 MW furnace-oil plants with capacity payments of about PKR 2.5 billion each; Nishat Power's smaller share count gives it a higher per-share figure.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The Nishat Chunian power plant is contracted to 2035.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Saif Power has the strongest willingness to pay dividends in the analyst's comparison, with a consistent twelve-year payout record, but no excess cash on its balance sheet; its contract expires in 2040.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A rising net receivable per share can mean either that the government has not paid the IPP or that the sponsor simply prefers not to distribute cash, so investors should not assume buying the share changes payout policy.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's stated rule is to invest in a power company only when conservatively estimated dividends over the next two years are about half the share price, so the dividend alone delivers the return and downside re-rating risk is limited.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst warns that overpaying for a dividend stock cuts both ways: if the payout comes in below expectation the market re-rates the share down on the lower yield, and the price loss can exceed the dividend received.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst attributes Pakgen Power's rally mainly to the Nishat group not holding a majority stake, with investors betting the sponsor must eventually buy control at any price, rather than to fundamentals.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Converting an existing plant to a different fuel does not raise an IPP's return rate: the company simply earns the regulated return on whatever additional investment it makes, so conversion rumours are weak value drivers.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When only about 80 percent of power invoices are recovered, a heavily dispatched plant's payment mostly covers fuel and debt service while its actual profit gets trapped in circular debt, so lightly run plants are paid relatively better.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: An IPP's fuel contract fixes the cost it may pass through, so as a plant ages and its heat rate degrades beyond the benchmark, every extra hour of running subtracts from profit instead of adding to it.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst argues power circular debt is far harder to solve than gas circular debt because power costs are high and distribution losses large, and sees no fix short of ending the single-buyer model and privatising the Discos.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: When a listed company is sold in Pakistan, minority shareholders must be offered book value, which the analyst cites as the reason a listed power company's shares re-rated before the SECP changed those rules.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'BEST POWER SECTOR COMPANIES TO INVEST IN' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Index returns hide wide dispersion: in 2025 the KSE-100 returned roughly 52 percent while Engro Fertilizers returned about 11 percent and Meezan Bank about 85 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Year-on-year inflation in Pakistan reached about 38 percent in May 2023, an experience the analyst cites as the reason many savers turned to gold and foreign currency.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst insists on converting 'my money doubled' into a compounded annual rate: a plot that doubles in ten years is only about 7.2 percent a year before transaction costs and taxes, and must be set against inflation.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: To compare property with shares the analyst insists on matching four things: holding period, income generated, total costs including taxes and transaction fees, and liquidity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A lower share price is not a discount: if a cement stock falls from 100 to 80 while sustainable EPS drops from 20 to 8, the P/E rises from 5 to 10 times and each rupee of earnings costs more than before.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst checks dispatches, selling price, energy cost, debt and expansion economics for a cement company, and sustainable earnings, deposit cost, asset quality and capital position for a bank.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For a dividend payer the analyst checks whether the payout is funded by recurring cash generation or by temporary income, and warns against capitalising one exceptionally profitable year's earnings forever.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst treats a person's job or family business as part of portfolio exposure, warning that holding shares in the same industry concentrates risk even if the number of stocks held is large.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst cautions that inflation does not automatically favour equities: only companies able to raise product prices protect margins, so the effect of inflation on sales, margins and cash flows must be assessed company by company.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst distinguishes information from value: knowing a company is building a factory is information, while the shareholder return depends on how it is funded, when profit starts and whether the market has already priced it.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Are You Investing Based on Facts or Feelings? How to Make Better Decisions with Your Money' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistani government securities are treasury bills of 3 to 12 months, issued at a discount as zero-coupon instruments, and longer Pakistan Investment Bonds of 3 to 15 years or more that pay fixed or floating coupons every 3 to 6 months.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan's New InvestPak Portal: What Investors Need to Know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: At the InvestPak launch it was stated that commercial banks hold roughly 78 percent of investment in Pakistani government securities, making them the sovereign's dominant creditor.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan's New InvestPak Portal: What Investors Need to Know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because lending to the government is safe and needs no credit assessment, banks park most of their funds in T-bills and bonds, which starves private-sector borrowers of credit and slows private investment growth.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan's New InvestPak Portal: What Investors Need to Know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The State Bank's InvestPak portal lets retail savers buy government securities directly from PKR 5,000 using only a local rupee bank account, part of a deliberate effort to diversify government funding away from banks.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan's New InvestPak Portal: What Investors Need to Know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The State Bank changed its minimum deposit rate rules so banks are no longer bound to a fixed profit-sharing rate on savings accounts holding more than PKR 10 million, letting them negotiate or set that rate themselves.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan's New InvestPak Portal: What Investors Need to Know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The Ministry of Finance, the State Bank and JS Cash introduced a T-bill investment option for JazzCash-style wallet users in mid-2026, though initially only three-month bills were offered.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Pakistan's New InvestPak Portal: What Investors Need to Know' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Image Pakistan is a women's clothing retailer whose lead product is premium embroidered one-size lawn wear, sold through its own stores and online.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Sales grew from roughly PKR 400 million a year in 2020, when the company had two or three stores, to an expected PKR 6 billion in FY26, roughly a fifteen-fold increase.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because its lead product is premium, the brand kept growing through Pakistan's 2023 and 2024 purchasing-power squeeze, and premium positioning supports gross margins of roughly 40 to 50 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst identifies design capability, driven largely by a young non-executive director involved in brand creation, as the company's main competitive advantage rather than scale or cost.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: About 75 percent of sales come from physical stores and 25 percent online, the online share including international orders from South Asian diaspora customers.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In branded eventwear most online orders are placed one or two days before a celebration, so delivery within 24 hours is critical - orders arriving in 48 to 72 hours are often refused by the customer.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The company opened an Amazon store in 2021 but set up its own international subsidiaries instead, because Amazon's return policies and courier-collected duties at the customer's door hurt service quality.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Online order data shows where demand is concentrated, and the company uses it to choose new store locations - a method the analyst credits for 14 stores opened without a single closure.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The company's two largest costs are fabric and embroidery-related wages, and its rent-to-sales ratio is comparatively low.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The company had no in-house embroidery machines until 2021 and outsourced the work; it now runs about ten schiffli and embroidery machines with another ten ordered, giving it direct control of product quality.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Stock in trade has risen past PKR 2.5 billion, which the analyst reads as roughly a full year of forward sales sitting in raw or finished inventory - far more than the three to four months a seasonal collection should need.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Management's own expansion arithmetic is that one or two new stores generating about PKR 1 billion of sales need roughly USD 1 million of capex plus PKR 600 million of working capital.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The long working capital cycle forced two rights issues in three years, roughly doubling the share count, so growth has been funded by dilution rather than internal cash and return on invested capital is depressed.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's general rule is that the best businesses minimise the working capital cycle so that growth does not require ever more capital, because a long cycle becomes a hurdle and depresses return on invested capital.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On a track record of 30-35 percent annual growth the analyst models FY26 revenue near PKR 6 billion, gross profit of PKR 2.5 billion, profit before tax around PKR 1.75 billion and profit after tax of PKR 1-1.25 billion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst notes the company pays no regular dividend as a growth business, and argues a fixed working capital cycle could justify a higher multiple than the market-level 7-8 times he applies.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Future growth options the analyst identifies are new categories sold through existing outlets - unstitched, western wear, perfumes - leveraging the existing loyal customer base and retail footprint.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst follows Peter Lynch's approach of treating a crowded shop in a mall as a leading indicator, since more customers now means higher sales and profits later.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's 'bull market framework' claim is that when Pakistan's economy is stable the market historically delivers roughly 30 to 35 percent average returns and the odds of a sharp devaluation are low.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Image Pakistan - All You Need to know about Pakistan's Fastest Growing Women Clothing Brand' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan consumes around 60 billion litres of milk a year, over half a litre per person per day, making dairy one of the country's largest consumer industries, with four listed players on the exchange.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fauji Foods sells milk, cheese, butter and ghee under the Nurpur brand, which dates to 1966; dairy contributes about 90 percent of revenue and Fauji Cereals, consolidated from 2024, another 7 to 8 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The company owns no dairy farm, so buying loose milk plus packaging make up about 90 percent of its cost of sales, with distribution and brand advertising the other significant cost lines.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Losses up to 2022 stemmed from gross underutilisation: the plant could process 200 million litres of milk a year but was running only about 40 million litres.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The turnaround from 2023 began with management hired from a top FMCG company, who lifted the retail outlet count from about 18,000 to 35,000 within a year and a half.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Solar for electricity, a biomass plant for steam and localised packaging together cut the company's annual costs by roughly PKR 1 to 2 billion, alongside renegotiated supplier contracts.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The company onboarded B2B customers including KFC, Pizza Hut, Hardee's and the OG Burger chain to soak up spare plant capacity.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's rule for a turnaround is to trace which specific strategy produced each period's improvement and model the new economics, rather than assuming improving numbers will keep improving.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In Pakistani FMCG, cost per pack falls as a product is placed in more outlets, and distribution economics only work well once a company reaches roughly 80,000 to 100,000 outlets.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Distribution reach differs sharply among Pakistani food companies: Nestle's products are in roughly 150,000 outlets and National Foods in about 80,000 to 90,000.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Even after doubling its outlet count the company runs at only about 35 percent of plant capacity, which is why management set a PKR 100 billion sales vision for 2029.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The company signed a contract with China's Royal Group to export buffalo milk, obtained the food export approvals, and began shipments around late 2024 and early 2025.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst models about PKR 35 billion of revenue and PKR 2-2.5 billion operating profit over the next year, with debt largely repaid, giving EPS near PKR 0.5-0.6 and, at a 20 times food-sector multiple, a fair value around PKR 12.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: As margin benchmarks the analyst cites Nestle Pakistan at roughly 17-18 percent operating margin overall and perhaps 13-14 percent on milk, and Olpers' owner at about 8-10 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: On a 2029 scenario of PKR 100 billion sales with operating margin 4-5 points higher from scale, the analyst gets PKR 10-12 billion operating profit, EPS near PKR 2.7-3 and a fair value of roughly PKR 55-60 at 20 times.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For a rapidly growing company the analyst values it twice: once on next year's earnings and once on the management's multi-year vision with improved unit economics, since brand value also builds with scale.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: About 90 percent of milk consumed in Pakistan is loose milk sold by informal sellers who pay no sales or income tax, and because dairy inputs are all local there is no port-stage tax to narrow the gap.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The 18 percent sales tax plus other taxes on formal dairy creates a price gap of roughly PKR 100 per litre between loose and packaged milk, which in a low-income country keeps consumers in the informal channel.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst argues zero-rating packaged milk, as most countries do for an essential commodity, is the single biggest swing factor for formal dairy volume growth and market share against loose milk.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In early 2024 the company absorbed the affiliate that owned the Fauji Cereals products; cereals contribute only 7-8 percent of revenue but carry materially higher margins, making it a segment worth monitoring.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'All You Need to Know about Fauji Foods' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's windfall-profit theme targets companies earning abnormal profits from a regulatory quirk or unfair advantage, and his condition is to invest only when that advantage substantially raises the company's return on invested capital.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Fertilizer plants supplied from the Mari gas field earn profitability far above the rest of the industry, an example of a feedstock-driven windfall advantage.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Cement plants located outside Punjab, in KPK, enjoy materially higher profitability than their Punjab peers, another case of a structural regional advantage.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The minimum deposit rate did not apply to Islamic banks for roughly a decade after it was imposed on conventional banks around 2012-13, a regulatory asymmetry the analyst links to Meezan Bank compounding near 30 percent a year while conventional bank prices stagnated.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: GIDC was imposed in 2013-14 and the analyst notes Engro Fertilizers benefited for about seven years, until 2020, because it held fixed-price contracts while the levy raised competitors' costs.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Roughly PKR 3,000 billion of circular debt accumulated in Pakistan's gas sector, and the IMF programme now requires no new gas circular debt, with any build-up from LNG diversion to be recovered within the following six months.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's key monitor for exploration companies is cash profit conversion: OGDC and PPL re-rated from about 1.5-2 times earnings to roughly 5 times as their cash conversion reached 100 percent once circular debt was contained.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Oil and gas exploration is a high return-on-capital industry in Pakistan, so when circular debt is not an issue these companies historically trade above the market average multiple rather than below it.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst argues the gas distribution utilities only benefit durably from circular-debt resolution if gas theft is also stopped, since unaccounted-for gas is the root of their losses.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In April 2024 the government deregulated prices of non-essential medicines in Pakistan, letting pharmaceutical companies set those prices freely.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst argues the share of non-essential medicines in a pharma portfolio is a misleading metric: competition stopped many firms raising non-essential prices, while hardship cases allowed large increases on essential drugs, so brand pricing power is what matters.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Falling global commodity prices lower dollar costs of pharmaceutical raw materials, and with a stable rupee this feeds straight into lower input costs for Pakistani drug makers.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Falling interest rates work on cyclicals twice: demand-led volume lifts profit per unit for cars, bikes, cement, glass and steel, and the market simultaneously awards those profits a higher multiple.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In a rate-cut cycle the analyst prefers cyclicals with strong 10-20 year shareholder returns over loss-making companies whose profits would only come from lower finance cost, so long-term compounding continues alongside the upcycle.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Within cyclicals the analyst checks a different variable per sector: whether an automaker's model is number one in its category, how efficient a cement plant is, and what gas price a glass maker pays.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst treats Chinese automakers in Pakistan as sitting in two themes at once - high-return cyclicals and windfall beneficiaries - because cheap vehicle costs in China give them an additional advantage.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's three-step process is: read the business in detail and compute its return on invested capital; project profits and likely multiple two to three years out and back-solve the return; then check the company's twenty-year shareholder return as a sanity test on management.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's core premise is that over the long run a company's return on invested capital and its share price growth converge, because shareholder wealth creation tracks the wealth the business itself creates.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst notes a single company can belong to more than one investing theme at once, which strengthens the case rather than complicating it.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst illustrates compounding valuation drivers with pharma: price up, cost down and multiple up together move a share far more than any one of them alone.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP COMPANIES  IN 2025' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst sorts PSX holdings into six investing themes, arguing that allocating a portfolio by theme improves its risk-reward ratio and sets expectations for each holding's volatility and likely return.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's fast-grower theme covers early-stage local FMCG, IT, retail chains and emerging brands, where he frames the two-year outcome range as anything from a tenfold gain over five years to near-total loss if the business model fails.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst requires a fast-grower candidate to have already delivered at least 30 percent annual revenue and profit growth for a minimum of two years, refusing to invest on potential alone.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For a domestically focused fast grower the analyst wants market capitalisation of roughly PKR 10-20 billion, since very few Pakistani companies exceed 200 billion and growth above 30 percent becomes hard at that size; the cap does not apply to exporters because the global market is far larger.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst avoids capital-intensive fast growers because funding each successive plant tends to force repeated rights issues, diluting the multi-bagger potential even if growth is achieved.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst caps a single early-stage fast grower at 5 percent of the portfolio until the company has been followed for two to three years.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Off-the-book sales can make a small company's owners rich while minority shareholders gain nothing, so the analyst checks for them: supplying a multinational or running POS terminals across retail outlets lowers the likelihood, and market surveys help verify reputation.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Before buying a small company in a large business group, the analyst checks that sponsors are genuinely committed to that specific company, since execution and management attention matter as much as business economics.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's pricing discipline for fast growers is to pay no more than the market PE, but applied to forward, next-year earnings rather than trailing earnings.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's turnaround theme covers businesses that price their product at import parity, such as chemical producers, imported-fertilizer players and refineries, whose margins can jump for a year or two during a global shortage.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A local producer that sells at the landed cost of imports captures the full gain when the international price rises, because its own cost base does not change.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In 2020 hurricanes in the United States shut down major PVC producers accounting for a large share of global capacity, lifting PVC margins sharply and multiplying Engro Polymer's per-ton earnings while its costs were unchanged.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst notes Engro Polymer began paying dividends during its 2020 margin windfall, and that on the PSX starting a dividend is itself a value-realisation event.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In 2022 a port fire in Bangladesh halted hydrogen peroxide imports priced near USD 400 per ton, forcing buyers to Korea at about USD 800, which sharply raised the per-ton earnings of the local Pakistani producer.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: After the Russian invasion in 2022 diesel cracks, normally about USD 10-12 per barrel over crude, widened to roughly USD 40, lifting refinery earnings on diesel several times over.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For import-parity turnarounds the analyst tracks global margins weekly together with the economics behind them, new plants coming online and the expected normalisation date, so he can exit before profits roll over.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Because the turnaround theme is momentum investing on a maximum two-year horizon, the analyst does not average down on weakness and adds only after a quarterly result confirms the higher-profit trend.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A shift in dividend policy can itself trigger a re-rating, and because sponsors set such policies they usually persist two to three years, so the analyst waits for one or two quarters of confirmation before acting.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst does not count debt-to-equity conversions or management changes as turnarounds; a true turnaround needs either higher business earning power or value realisation through dividend policy.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's third theme is asset plays, acquisitions and delistings: deeply undervalued PSX companies where a sale or delisting unlocks value, approached with Mohnish Pabrai's heads-I-win, tails-I-do-not-lose-much principle because the margin of safety is already in the price.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For delistings and takeovers the analyst reads PSX and SECP rules closely because they specify what minority shareholders must be offered, and such transactions normally complete within a year.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst invests in a delisting or acquisition only once the company itself has made the information public, since the market constantly carries unverified takeover rumours.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For circular-debt names such as OGDC, PPL and power companies the analyst weighs both the gap between fair and market value and the probability the receivables are actually cleared, not the discount alone.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst is more confident of eventual payment to independent power producers, which he expects within about three years because the money is owed to private investors, than of government clearing dues to OGDC and PPL on any set timetable.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'TOP INVESTING THEMES - HOW TO INVEST LIKE A PRO' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Government securities are treasury bills, typically 3 to 12 months and sold at a discount to face value as zero-coupon instruments, and longer bonds of 3 to 15 years or more that pay coupons every three or six months at rates near the policy rate.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Commercial banks hold roughly 78 percent of Pakistan's government securities because lending to the sovereign is safe and needs no credit assessment, which crowds out private sector credit and leaves the government dependent on one funding source.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The State Bank launched InvestPark, a digital platform letting retail savers buy government securities from PKR 5,000, intended to diversify government borrowing away from banks and free bank balance sheets for private lending.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The State Bank changed minimum deposit rate rules so banks no longer must share profit at a fixed rate on savings accounts above PKR 10 million, which lowers payouts to large depositors and can push that money into government securities.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In mid-June 2026 the Ministry of Finance, State Bank and JS Cash enabled treasury bill investment for JS Cash users, initially limited to three-month bills.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst frames National Bank of Pakistan as a turnaround built on four factors: industry-leading deposit growth in 2025, resolution of the pension case uncertainty, abolition of the minimum deposit rate, and roughly PKR 2 trillion locked in at high interest rates.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: National Bank's 2024 earnings were only about PKR 12 per share because the whole pension case expense was booked in that one year, yet it still announced a PKR 8 dividend at the end of 2024, its first in many years.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: With about PKR 20 per share earned in the first half, the analyst projected National Bank's 2025 full-year earnings near PKR 38-40 per share and, on a 60-65 percent payout, a dividend of roughly PKR 24-26.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst gauges a bank's dividend-paying capacity from its capital adequacy ratio, which shows how much surplus equity it holds; National Bank standing near 30 percent implied room for a large payout.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: For 2026 the analyst modelled National Bank on a 10 percent average interest rate, roughly PKR 5 trillion of deposits and a 30 percent current account share, giving net interest income near PKR 260-265 billion.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's 2026 National Bank build used about PKR 125 billion of operating expenses and roughly PKR 10 billion of provisioning at half a percent of the book, giving pre-tax profit near PKR 175 billion and after-tax profit of PKR 85-90 billion, or about PKR 40-44 per share.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Pakistan's banking sector tax rate is scheduled to fall by one percentage point each year, mechanically lifting after-tax profits over time.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst builds a bank's forward earnings from average interest rates, deposit size and current account share to get net interest income, then adds fee income and subtracts operating expenses, provisioning and tax.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The State Bank now requires some provisioning against available-for-sale securities, mostly government bills and PIBs, phased over three years, which slightly reduces every bank's capital adequacy ratio.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: National Bank has already absorbed 30-50 percent of the required available-for-sale securities provisioning into its capital adequacy ratio while still holding around 30 percent.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Floods hit banks through their agriculture lending, but the analyst notes the 2022 floods caused little sector-wide loss because most such loans sit under government schemes that carry partial guarantees.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: National Bank has about PKR 120 billion lent to the agriculture sector, its main channel of flood exposure, and management expects its balance sheet to stay protected as in 2022.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: National Bank closed its New York branches and paid the imposed penalty, ending that case, and has also settled the related secondary liability claims, so the analyst sees little residual legal risk there.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst views it as favourable that National Bank's president and CEO is a long-time NBP employee who understands the bank from the ground up, with the turnaround now resting on deposit growth and branch revamp execution.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: National Bank was historically a reliable dividend payer and even raised its dividend in the 2008 financial crisis year, which the analyst cites in arguing it can return to that status.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's historical rule is that when Pakistan's macro indicators are moving in the right direction and the bull-market framework is on, the index averages 30-35 percent returns a year without rupee devaluation eroding them.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Major floods used to strike Pakistan roughly once every 10 to 15 years but two have occurred within five years, raising the baseline frequency of agricultural and household damage.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'My Strategy: What You might be missing.' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst argues local political drama rarely moves the PSX while reserves and macro indicators are healthy; the market reacts only when a final decision lands and reserves start falling, as during the Panama Papers process from 2014-15.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Imran Khan Release from Jail. Impact on PSX? Islamabad Trip!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: To judge whether a political accommodation is becoming more likely, the analyst watches confidence-building measures and the degree of resistance to creating new administrative units, rather than headlines about an initial deal.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Imran Khan Release from Jail. Impact on PSX? Islamabad Trip!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst stresses that anyone giving investment advice in Pakistan must hold SECP licences, and that three to four years of full-time company research is the realistic apprenticeship.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'Imran Khan Release from Jail. Impact on PSX? Islamabad Trip!' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst holds that each sector cannot be analysed without its governing policy documents: Auto Policy 2016 and 2021 for autos, the new refinery policy for refineries, and the petroleum policies for oil and gas companies.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'UNDERSTAND BUSINESS LIKE OWNERS & EARN LIKE TOP BUSINESSMEN OF PAKISTAN - FOR ALL RETAIL INVESTORS' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst treats financial numbers as the output of a business machine, so understanding the mechanism comes first and ratios and history only confirm it; future performance originates in the business model.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'UNDERSTAND BUSINESS LIKE OWNERS & EARN LIKE TOP BUSINESSMEN OF PAKISTAN - FOR ALL RETAIL INVESTORS' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst stresses that good results do not automatically lift a share price, so a separate question is when value is realised for minority shareholders, and that boom-bust cycles and politics must be built into position sizing.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'UNDERSTAND BUSINESS LIKE OWNERS & EARN LIKE TOP BUSINESSMEN OF PAKISTAN - FOR ALL RETAIL INVESTORS' (YouTube transcript, undated)
